questions.question: What actually happens in coronary heart disease?

options.text: Plaque builds up in the arteries that supply the heart
options.explanation: Right - that build-up is what narrows the arteries and reduces blood flow to the heart.

options.text: The heart becomes too large
options.explanation: Not quite - CHD is about narrowed arteries, not the size of the heart itself.

options.text: An infection in the heart valves
options.explanation: That describes a different condition. CHD is caused by plaque build-up in the coronary arteries.

questions.question: Which of these is a risk factor you CAN change?

options.text: Family history
options.explanation: Family history matters, but it's not something you can change.

options.text: Smoking
options.explanation: Right - quitting smoking is one of the most powerful changes you can make for your heart.

options.text: Age
options.explanation: Getting older is a real risk factor, but it isn't something you can change.

questions.question: According to Ethiopia's 2015 national survey, roughly how many adults have high blood pressure?

options.text: About 1 in 6
options.explanation: Correct - the survey found hypertension in about 15.8% of adults, close to 1 in 6.

options.text: About 1 in 100
options.explanation: The real figure is much higher - about 15.8%, not 1%.

options.text: About 1 in 2
options.explanation: That overstates it - the survey found about 15.8%, not 50%.

questions.question: Where is angina discomfort typically felt?

options.text: Behind the breastbone
options.explanation: Right - that's the typical location, though it can radiate elsewhere.

options.text: Only in the left foot
options.explanation: Angina is a chest symptom, not a foot symptom.

options.text: Only in the ears
options.explanation: That's not a typical location for angina.

questions.question: Which of these makes angina 'unstable' and a medical emergency?

options.text: It happens at rest, is new, or is more severe than usual
options.explanation: Right - any of these makes it unstable angina, which needs urgent care.

options.text: It happens only after climbing stairs
options.explanation: That pattern - predictable, exertion-related, and short-lived - describes stable angina, not unstable.

options.text: It goes away after 2 minutes of rest
options.explanation: Settling quickly with rest is a feature of stable angina, not unstable angina.

questions.question: Besides chest discomfort, which of these is a common accompanying sign?

options.text: Shortness of breath
options.explanation: Right - shortness of breath, cold sweat, and nausea often accompany angina or ACS.

options.text: Improved appetite
options.explanation: That's not a symptom associated with angina or ACS.

options.text: Better sleep
options.explanation: That's not a symptom associated with angina or ACS.

questions.question: Which of these is a LESS well-known heart attack sign, more common in women?

options.text: Jaw or back pain, sweating, or dizziness
options.explanation: Right - these signs are real but less well-known than chest pain, and are common in women.

options.text: Chest pain
options.explanation: Chest pain is the well-known sign, not the less-known one this question is asking about.

options.text: A runny nose
options.explanation: A runny nose is not a heart attack warning sign.

questions.question: What should you do if you notice heart attack warning signs?

options.text: Wait a few hours to see if it goes away on its own
options.explanation: Waiting hours risks serious harm - act promptly instead.

options.text: Tell someone right away, and call your emergency contact if it's severe or doesn't improve in about 10 minutes
options.explanation: Right - every minute matters when it comes to a heart attack.

options.text: Ignore it if you feel fine otherwise
options.explanation: Warning signs should never be ignored, even if you otherwise feel okay.

questions.question: Why does every minute matter during a heart attack?

options.text: The longer it takes to get help, the more the heart muscle can be damaged
options.explanation: Right - quick action limits the damage to the heart.

options.text: It doesn't - there's no rush
options.explanation: There is a real rush - delay increases the damage to the heart.

options.text: Only the first 24 hours matter
options.explanation: It's the first minutes, not the first day, that matter most.

questions.question: Is a heart-healthy eating pattern a strict, restrictive diet?

options.text: No - it's a pattern of foods chosen regularly, over time
options.explanation: Right - it's about a sustainable pattern, not a restrictive short-term diet.

options.text: Yes - you must cut out entire food groups
options.explanation: That's not how a heart-healthy eating pattern works - it's about balance, not elimination.

options.text: Yes - it means eating the same single meal every day
options.explanation: There's real variety in a heart-healthy pattern - it isn't one repeated meal.

questions.question: Which is a good example of the 'protein-rich foods' step?

options.text: Shiro, misir, and kik most days, with fish
options.explanation: Right - legumes and fish are the best options, with smaller amounts of eggs and lean meat.

options.text: Fried food every day
options.explanation: Fried food is not part of the recommended protein-rich pattern.

options.text: Only red meat every day
options.explanation: Lean red meat should be limited, not eaten daily as the main protein source.

questions.question: What's the easiest way to cut down on salt?

options.text: Choose fresh, unprocessed foods and flavour with herbs and spices instead
options.explanation: Right - processed and packaged foods are the biggest source of hidden salt.

options.text: Add extra salt to make food taste better
options.explanation: That increases salt intake, which raises blood pressure risk - the opposite of the goal.

options.text: Eat more canned and packaged food
options.explanation: Canned and packaged foods are usually high in salt, not a way to reduce it.

questions.question: How much moderate activity is recommended most days of the week?

options.text: 30-60 minutes
options.explanation: Right - that's the recommended range, built up gradually from a smaller starting point.

options.text: 5 hours
options.explanation: That's far more than the recommended amount - start smaller and build up.

options.text: None - rest is always better
options.explanation: Regular activity, not rest, is what reduces heart disease risk.

questions.question: What's a good way to stay motivated to be active?

options.text: Choose activities you enjoy and involve friends or family
options.explanation: Right - enjoyment and social support both help activity stick.

options.text: Only do activities you dislike, to build discipline
options.explanation: Disliking an activity makes it much harder to keep doing - enjoyment matters.

options.text: Wait until you feel highly motivated before starting
options.explanation: Starting small and building the habit works better than waiting for motivation to appear.

questions.question: Why does sitting less matter, even if you exercise sometimes?

options.text: People who sit less throughout the day have a lower risk of early death
options.explanation: Right - reducing sitting time throughout the day is its own separate benefit.

options.text: It doesn't matter as long as you exercise once a week
options.explanation: Time spent sitting through the rest of the day matters on its own, separate from exercise sessions.

options.text: Sitting is always better for the heart
options.explanation: Prolonged sitting is linked to higher risk, not lower.

questions.question: Why might a prevention medication feel like it's 'doing nothing'?

options.text: It works silently in the background to prevent future problems, without an obvious day-to-day feeling
options.explanation: Right - that's exactly how prevention medications work, unlike symptom-relief ones.

options.text: Because it genuinely does nothing and can be stopped safely
options.explanation: Feeling nothing doesn't mean it isn't working - stopping it can undo real protection.

options.text: Because only symptom-relief medications actually work
options.explanation: Both kinds of medication do real work - they just work in different, sometimes invisible, ways.

questions.question: What should you do before stopping or changing a heart medication?

options.text: Talk to your clinician first
options.explanation: Right - never change or stop a heart medication on your own.

options.text: Just stop it once you feel better
options.explanation: Feeling better is often a sign the medication is working, not a signal to stop it.

options.text: Ask a friend or family member for advice instead
options.explanation: This decision needs your clinician, who knows your full medical picture.

questions.question: What is the job of a symptom-relief heart medication?

options.text: Easing the heart's workload to reduce chest pain and allow more activity
options.explanation: Right - that's the symptom-relief job, distinct from disease-prevention.

options.text: Curing coronary heart disease completely
options.explanation: No current medication cures CHD outright - these medications manage and reduce risk.

options.text: Replacing the need for a heart-healthy lifestyle
options.explanation: Medication works alongside diet, activity, and other lifestyle changes - not instead of them.

questions.question: About how much more likely is a smoker to die of a heart attack or stroke?

options.text: About four times more likely
options.explanation: Right - that's the real increase in risk from smoking.

options.text: Not more likely at all
options.explanation: Smoking substantially raises this risk - it isn't neutral.

options.text: About four times LESS likely
options.explanation: It's the opposite direction - smoking increases the risk, not decreases it.

questions.question: What does the 'D' in 'Delay' mean in the 5 D's technique?

options.text: Wait out the craving, even briefly - it will pass
options.explanation: Right - a craving is temporary, and delaying gives it time to fade.

options.text: Decide to smoke later instead of now
options.explanation: Delay means waiting out the urge without smoking, not postponing a cigarette.

options.text: Give up on quitting for the day
options.explanation: Delay is about getting through one craving, not giving up on the whole attempt.

questions.question: How soon does heart attack and stroke risk start to drop after quitting?

options.text: Almost straight away
options.explanation: Right - the risk reduction begins quickly, which is real encouragement to quit.

options.text: Only after 10 years
options.explanation: The benefit starts much sooner than that, even though full risk reduction builds over time.

options.text: It never changes once you've smoked
options.explanation: Quitting does genuinely lower risk, starting soon after you stop.
